messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Sparsity detection for ODE systems possible?
parts:
Hi!

I am trying to understand where the ODE system of Stan has areas for improvements. I learned that the coupled ODE system does not explore sparsity, i.e. I am considering a standard 2-cmt oral dosing ODE, see code below. The ODE has 3 equations and only 4 parameters. The coupled ODE system in Stan has size 24 (I placed a cout into the code to find out), while to my understanding from the structure of the system far less are needed, i.e.

3 ODEs base system
3 sensitivities for the initial value
1 sensitivity for dy1/dka dka/dt
4 sensitivites for dy2 (all parameters)
2 sensitivites for dy3/dt

= in total only 13

I hope my understanding here is correct (counting of the sensitivities). I mean passing 11 sensitivities into the ODE integrator which are always zero will certainly make it slow down. Moreover, using a better ODE integrator which calculates the Jacobian (for stiff regions) will be much more costly for higher dimensional systems, I think.

Of course, I don't know how hard it is to detect the sparsity with the magic auto-diff being done here, but if this is possible without too much of a hassle, this will give a large performance boost, especially for large systems.

Best,
Sebastian


real[] twoCmtOral_ode(real t,
real[] y,
real[] theta,
real[] x_r,
int[] x_i) {
real dydt[3];
real ka;
real k12;
real k21;
real k10;

ka <- theta[1];
k10 <- theta[2];
k12 <- theta[3];
k21 <- theta[4];

dydt[1] <- -ka * y[1];
dydt[3] <- k12 * y[2] - k21 * y[3];
dydt[2] <- -dydt[1] - k10 * y[2] -dydt[3];

return dydt;
}

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Sparsity detection for ODE systems possible?
parts:
The autodiff's expensive, but I don't know how much
all-zero systems will slow things down.

I don't know that there's a good way to detect sparsity.
All our autodiff does is compute a gradient at a point.
In general, detecting sparsity is a hard problem because you
need the symbolic math.

One alternative might be to have user-defined sensitivities.
It'll be error prone, but it can be fast.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Sparsity detection for ODE systems possible?
parts:
I understood from Frederic that lsoda uses a lot of effort to detect sparsity. So this seems to be important. Ok, ultimately a benchmark would be needed here.

If user-defined sensitivities are an option, then coupling this with a system like Theano will make this fairly robust - i.e. I mean that a standardized Theano script could write out some standardized representation of the needed sensitivities (I am not suggesting an integration of Stan with Theano here, just to emphasize).

As the ODE systems often have really simple algebraic structure, this should be possible for most ODE systems.

Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Sparsity detection for ODE systems possible?
parts:
I played around with deSolve in R to check what the overhead is due to integrating zero: Looks like it is about 20% of a performance hit when you add 10 dummy equations to 3 equations of a 2cmt system.

Also of interest for R users is the cOde package which does symbolic differentiation of ODE systems and can generate automatically C files which contain the ODE functor along with the ODE sensitivities (and the hessian if needed) fully automatically. This way deSolve in R runs very fast. So getting the sensitivities from the user error free should be possible without a too high error rate.

Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Sparsity detection for ODE systems possible?
parts:
> On Aug 24, 2015, at 9:55 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I played around with deSolve in R to check what the overhead is due to integrating zero: Looks like it is about 20% of a performance hit when you add 10 dummy equations to 3 equations of a 2cmt system.

That's not too surprising since you always get good accuracy and
any step size works in that dimension.

Unfortunately, the overhead in Stan's going to be higher because of
all the autodiff that gets done to create that zero.

Any hints on how lsoda detects sparsity? The code all-in isn't that
long, but I haven't gone through it.

In any case, the first step's going to be getting a solid stiff
solver in with control over tolerances.

> Also of interest for R users is the cOde package which does symbolic differentiation of ODE systems and can generate automatically C files which contain the ODE functor along with the ODE sensitivities (and the hessian if needed) fully automatically. This way deSolve in R runs very fast. So getting the sensitivities from the user error free should be possible without a too high error rate.

That's an interesting idea for simple ODE systems --- I often use symbolic
differentiation myself when writing Stan functions. I find Wolfram Alpha online
to be super helpful. But I still don't know of anything that'll work for matrix
equations and reduce them to matrix equations.

- Bob

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Sparsity detection for ODE systems possible?
parts:
Nope, I have no idea on sparsity detection in lsoda (and I am only citing Frederic, he may know more). If I were to guess, then it is some (clever) heuristic.

You mention that autodiff is so expensive, if I read the code which get's generated from Stan right, then the ODE system is for every iteration auto-diffed to get the coupled system. I may read that wrong, of course - and also I guess that the autodiff cost is low in comparison to solving the ODE...

And yes, cOde is a neat solution for fast simulation of ODEs in R. Possibly useful in a Stan context. And most ODE systems will have simple algebraic structure. What is already difficult is if you get a Michaelis-Menten term ala

dy/dt = - Km * y/(y + Vm)

Indeed, the largest problem with the ODE stuff seems to be the occasional lockups of the RK integrator in stiff regions. No way around lsoda or cvode I guess.

Also, if the integrator were to support events (dosing stuff), then one could avoid integrating in steps which requires to make the initial value as parameter. This way the sensitivities for the initial values won't be needed.

Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Sparsity detection for ODE systems possible?
parts:
I'm not sure how low the cost of autodiff is compared to solving
the ODE. The system's autodiffed w.r.t. parameters every time the
system function is called.

I don't see how we'd be able to build something like dosing into
the integrator itself or how that would avoid sensitivities for initial
values --- if the initial values are known, we don't need sensitivities,
if they're not known, then we'll have to calculate them.

These algorithms are iterative and do lots of calls to the system function
per solution, so if you only mean the very first step, I don't think that's
going to be a big deal.

- Bob

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Sparsity detection for ODE systems possible?
parts:
Hi Bob!

The repeated autodiffing of the system function could be a possibility for optimization where a user-defined sensitivity system would also help, sure (or caching of the autodiff stack if this is possible).

Having an event capable ODE integrator helps in the following way: Currently, I step through the data set from event to event and each time I restart the integrator with a new initial state which is state of the system function at the time point when a new event is encountered.

Since the event history is fixed with the data as is the initial state at time point 0, the sensitivities for the initial time point is not needed if the integrator were to process things with events in a single sweep.

Concretely, in a PK system with dosing: The initial state is always 0 in all compartments (no drug ever administered). The history of dosing events is fixed with the data and hence no sensitivities are needed for the initials. However in the current design I have to integrate in steps and restart the integrator at each dosing event with the initial set to the amounts in the compartments at the time of the dosing event.

Not having the initials as parameters considerably reduces the coupled system size.

Sebastian

state is going to be a parameter in Stan terms, so sensitivities
will get computed. It'll be even worse when we need Jacobians for
stiff systems.

There's nothing in place to cache an autodiff stack. I agree that
having fixed symbolic derivatives is always going to be a win
computationally if we can figure out how to include them.

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Sparsity detection for ODE systems possible?
parts:
Was I wrong with my understanding? I.e. using an event integrator allows me to set the initial initial to zero hence avoiding those sensitivities.

For stiff systems the sparsity may become more of a burden due to the exploding Jacobian.

An elegant solution could be to introduce a DSL for specifying ODEs. Then the ODE can be parsed at compile time into whatever is suitable for Stan to solve it. This is similar to what cOde does and possibly such a thing exists already somewhere which is closer to C++. No idea how much effort this is.

Fixed symbolic derivatives from the user (possibly with a way to indicate sparsity) is maybe a good compromise - and could be superseded by a more elegant thing.

Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Sparsity detection for ODE systems possible?
parts:
Hi Bob!

ODE DSL: I meant something very simple (like the simple cODE R package), i.e. something which takes input like

y1' = -ka * y1
y2' = ka * y1 - Km * y2/(y2 + Vm)

and then derives from this text representation whatever sensitives and Jacobians are needed (symbolically) as C++ code (maybe PyStan coupled with Theano would be a good first attempt).

As a first step, one could implement something in Stan which takes user-defined sensitivities which could be used in a more elegant approach as backend for such an ODE DSL thing.

Resources... yep, hopefully these can be found.

Sebastian
